name: Rhodamine Purple
lede: Rhodamine Purple is a vivid pink-purple named for rhodamine, a brightly fluorescent dye the Swiss chemist Maurice Ceresole synthesized in 1887.

sections.title: Named for the Greek word for rose
sections.body:
Ceresole made the first rhodamine dye in 1887 by heating a mix of two coal-tar compounds in the presence of an acid catalyst, and named the resulting class "rhodamines" from the Greek *rhodon*, rose, for their intense rose-red color [3]. The dyes were marketed commercially within a year and prized for staying bright and stable in light far longer than the fluorescein dyes before them [3]. Rhodamine B, the best known member, is still used today as a biological stain and, more controversially, as an illegal food colorant in some countries [3].

Ridgway's 1912 atlas lists this particular tone on plate XII, hue 67, and the ISCC-NBS 1955 revision places it in block 254, "vivid purplish red" [1]. In LCH terms it measures lightness 48, chroma 75, hue 345, one of the most saturated colors in our library, nearest to [[red-violet|Red-Violet]], [[fandango|Fandango]] and [[byzantine|Byzantine]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds essentially no match for this intense pink-purple: across 23,781 paintings, none clear the five-percent coverage threshold our matching uses, as photographed [2]. That absence fits the color's own origin story: rhodamine is a synthetic dye too vivid and too recent for any pre-twentieth-century pigment to have reproduced on canvas [2][3]. The screen swatch shown here is best read as a reference color rather than a shade that historical painters had access to [2].

questions.q: The word "rhodamine" comes from a Greek word meaning what?
True or false: our painting archive finds this exact color commonly, because rhodamine dyes were widely used by painters.

openers: Rhodamine Purple is so vivid, and so recent, that our 23,781-painting archive barely finds it anywhere.
